en: I shall now fully proclaim the *kārikā*: first, that which is technical (*pāribhāṣika*);
then, that concerning the *saṃhitā*; thereafter, the fruit of the complete recitation (*vedapārāyaṇa*) of the Veda;
as well as the sequence of recitation, the function of speech, and the characteristics of words.
Now, the characteristics of *krama*, *jaṭā*, and *śuddhavarṇakrama* are given in due order; therein, the rules for the two types of doubling (*dvitvāgama*) that are traditionally taught,
as well as for *abhinidhāna* and the doubling known as *kevala*, are explained.

The definition of the *yamas* and their prohibitions (*pratiṣedhas*), the two types of *dvirāgama* (doubling) and their prohibitions, the definitions of the *svarabhaktis* along with their examples and technical names (4),
the definition of *vivṛtti* (vowel opening), and the technical names and examples for that— [these are explained].
The nasal sound situated between the *vyakti* [vowels] belongs to both the protracted (*pluta*) and long (*dīrgha*) vowels known as *raṅga*;

it is specifically the characteristic of the *svarita*, *udātta*, and tremulous (*kampita*) accents, as well as of the modified (*vaikṛta*) and natural (*prākṛta*) nasals, and the chest-born (*aurasya*) sounds. 5–6.

The rules for the placement of the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya, as well as the rules for euphonic combination (sandhi), and likewise the characteristics of the *praṇava*; the sequence of vowels and consonants therein, and the description of the acute (*udātta*) and other accents.

The definition of the seven accents accompanied by examples (8); the distinctions of effort (prayatna), as well as the sequence of measures (mātrā) and phonemes (varṇa), the determination of the measurement of measures, and the rules for the expression of the duration of measures (9).
In that regard, there is the sequence of the description of the limbs, the characteristics of the limbs of those previously mentioned by others,
and from that sequence of the description of the limbs, the characteristics become very clear; furthermore,
there is the etymological explanation of the sequence of colors which constitutes the essence of the colors.

The enumeration of the properties of phonemes (varṇadharma), their sequential order as explained therein, the description of the secondary vowels (bhakti), the anusvāra, and the kampita, as well as the nature of the vocalization of musical notes (raṅga), the manner of the production of sound, and the definition of resonance (dhvani) are treated there. 11–12.
Therein is situated within the body that which is characterized by all activities:

the maintenance of the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), the locations and movements of the five vital airs (pañcavāyu), the various types of sounds, and the determination of the phonemes produced therein. 13.
However, the distinction between their places and articulators is of that same kind [as the distinction between phonemes].

The differences in effort for the phonemes consist of the designations of deities and classes; likewise, the deities, classes, and qualities of the accents such as the acute (udātta) and others are also [distinguished by these]. 14–15.

Then follows the definition of the placement of the hand-sounds (hasta-svara-nyāsa) and its fruit; the description of the seven notes beginning with Ṣaḍja according to the sixfold states of the limbs and so forth (16);
the origin of the accents such as Udātta and the greatness of the Veda.
The fruit of studying the Veda when conjoined with the eightfold phonetic modifications (vikṛti) [is as follows]. 17.
Thus, in this sequence, the Śīkṣā is now fully proclaimed. 18.
Thus ends the Ātreyī-Śīkṣā-Kārikā.
Having bowed to that Supreme Light, whose utterances are the traditional scriptures and whose two eyes are the moon and the sun, I shall declare this stainless instruction on phonetics (śikṣā). 1.
Vowels are called *ac*, while consonants are known as *hal*. Among the vowels,

the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) forms of the letters *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*— namely *a ā*, *i ī*, *u ū*, *ṛ ṝ*, and *ḷ*— as well as *e ai*, *o au*, and the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* (the *aḥkāra*), are to be understood as the vowels.

Ka-kha-ga-gha-ṅa, ca-cha-ja-jha-ña, ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa, ta-tha-da-dha-na, pa-pha-bha-ma—these are the twenty-five *sparśa* (stops). Ya-ra-la-va are the four *antasthā* (semivowels). Ca-cha-ja-jha-ña, ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa, ta-tha-da-dha-na, pa-pha-bha-ma, ya-ra-la-va, śa-ṣa-sa-ha—these are the [remaining] consonants. 3–4.

The six sibilants (ūṣman), the visarga, the anusvāra, and the five beginning with *la*— these fifty-nine phonemes of the Yajurveda have been declared. In their respective order, there are five groups of the stops (sparśa) which are designated as "classes" (varga).

Among those groups, the designations for the first four are "first" (prathama) and so forth; for the fifth, "last" (uttama) is prescribed. Among the *kṛta* consonants, the voiced and unvoiced are indeed [the first two]; the sibilants (*ūṣman*), the first [unaspirated] stops, and the visarga are the second.
Those other than these are voiceless (*aghoṣa*), while the consonants (*hal*) are traditionally remembered as voiced (*ghoṣavat*).
*Parivi*, *nyābhi*, *upa*, *pra*, *ava*, *prati*, *adhi*, and *upasarga* [are prefixes].
The term "vowel" (*svara*) is explained as that which follows the sound *kāra* and consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *r*.

The classification of consonants (*vyañjana*) consists of the groups beginning with *cha*, *ṣa*, and *sa*; likewise, among the vowels (*svara*), there are the short *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*, as well as *lṛ*.
Furthermore, the last letter of each group (*varga*) is called the "end of the group," while the first is called the "beginning of the group. 9–10.
Thus ends the *Ātreya-Śikṣā-paribhāṣā*.
Regarding the subject of the *saṃhitā*:
that which constitutes a branch (*śākhā*) of the *Yajus* at its commencement is known as a *saṃhitā*.

Those other Yajurveda branches which are divided internally by sections (*kāṇḍa*), questions (*praśna*), chapters (*anuvāka*), and so forth— one should not recite their *saṃhitā* text, nor their specific *pada* and *krama* arrangements. (11–12)

The sequences of matted locks (jaṭā), colors (varṇa), and steps (krama) are traditionally known as the successive transformations; likewise, there are those joined with simple vowels, those accompanied by the mātrikās, those with their limbs (sāṅga), those which are the essence of letters (varṇasāra), and the five sequences of letters (pañcavarṇakrama). 13. These are difficult [to master].
The Veda, which is to be understood through all its constituent parts, should be studied from a written text; however,
that [Veda] which is the fruit of the complete mastery of the Vedas must be studied with effort by the twice-born from the mouth of a guru.

In the Vedas, every single syllable is individually a name of Hari. Whatever the phonetic combination (saṃhitā) may be—neither deficient in accent nor in letter—the fruit that is said here to result from reciting it once in its entirety (pārāyaṇa) is as follows: 15–16.

The sequence of the *pārāyaṇa* is threefold in that state; therefore, in this sequence it becomes eightfold. It is said to be one hundredfold in the chapter on matted hair (*jaṭādhyāya*), and one thousandfold in the pure phoneme (*śuddhavarṇa*). 17.
One should know that [the merit] is a *svaravarṇa* when joined with a *vidyā*, a *niyuta* when joined with a *mātrikā*,
a *prayuta* when joined with an *aṅgavarṇa*, and it becomes infinite (*ananta*) when joined with a *varṇasāraka*.
This applies in the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the *kṛcchra* penance, in the *brahmayajña*, and in the ritual procedures.
One should perform the recitation of the *saṃhitā* according to the rules, not that of individual words and so forth (19).
However, when the Lord of Gods has emerged from the womb for the sake of a festival,
one may recite the *krama-pāṭha* and so on, or likewise recite the *upaniṣads* (20).

But he who, abandoning the *pārāyaṇa* out of fear of missing the appointed time, performs the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) without the ritual acts, should be known as a sinner in that regard. Even when the great hour of dusk has arrived, one should then perform it in the presence of the Lord of Gods.
One should not abandon the study of the Vedas for even a single month, nor should one abandon the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*).
If one should abandon it out of delusion, then one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).
Thus ends the first chapter.
Regarding the activity of speech, there are three modes of speech: fast, medium, and slow.
Having repeated [the text] again and again in practice, the twice-born should recite it with the fast mode of speech.
For the purpose of recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), one should employ the medium speed;
however, for the purpose of instructing disciples, one should adopt the slow speed.
This is the definition of the *pada*.

In the section on words (padādhyāya), when the word *yad* is employed at the end of a word (*padānte*) and is then uttered again in two ways, that is known as a "circumferential word" (*veṣṭanapada*). A word accompanied by such circumferentiality is called *iṅgya*.
For the meaning of a word is "indicated" (*iṅgyate*), and for this reason it is called "indicated" (*iṅgya*);
the meaning of a word that possesses division is not displaced from its division. Thus is the meaning of the term *iṅgya*; however, its prior [form] is the *avagraha*.
The ten beginning with *pary* are declared to be prepositional words (*upasarga-pada*).
Together with the nine words beginning with *anu*, *apa*, *ā*, *pi*, *su*, *ut*, *sam*, *niḥ*, and *parā*, these words total nineteen. (28–29)
The first syllable of two words at the end of a sentence is elided; the middle one of three is elided.
Here, in the case of *avagraha*, that which ends in *na* is not elided; thus [the word] would be *adhvarā*.
Those which are *pragrahas* according to the characteristics [of the rules] are those that end in a vowel when followed by a word.
One should recite the characteristics of the *krama* method like the *saṃhitā*, first repeating two words in succession;
there, one should conclude the second word as if it were at the end of a pause.

Then, having omitted the first word, one should recite the second and the third; thereafter, having omitted that second word, one should recite the third and the fourth. Afterward, one should recite again in this very same sequence. 32–33.
Having released each preceding word and joined it with each succeeding one, that which is thus uttered is called the *kramādhyāya*.
In the *krama* [recitation], when the preceding word is thus uttered according to its sequence, [it is joined with the following]. 34.
In the *krama*, while the preceding word is being uttered in that manner, [it is joined with the next].
Having recited the *veṣṭana*, one should subsequently recite it according to the proper sequence (35).

Whatever concludes the preceding section (*pūrvavākya*) and likewise begins the subsequent section (*paravākya*), one should not omit that [junction] between the final part of the former and the initial part of the latter *anuvāka* (36).

If the first word should be joined with a *pragraha* and an *aniṅgya*, it is to be wrapped around as a single unit; however, that which is *aniṅgya* at the end of the sentence [is treated separately].
But if a word ends in *yad* or *yat*, one should recite it in sequence ending in *na*.

One should always recite [the word] together with the suffixes *ṣaṇ*, *tva*, and *ta* according to the prescribed rule (38). If a word ending in *-a* has a raised accent (*udātta*) at its end and is preceded by a prefix, there should be a "triple-step" (*trikrama*) over it; however, if the following word begins with *naḥ*, the step should be downward (39).
Having followed the three words and then omitted the first word, one should again utter the middle and the last words; thus one should speak in sequence during the triple-step.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Having first recited the *jaṭā* according to the direct order (*anuloma*), one should then recite it in reverse order (*pratiloma*);
then, having joined them together, one should again perform the recitation of the two words in their sequential order. 41.
Thus, that which is the order of recitation is proclaimed as "jaṭā" (the matted hair).
Whatever has been stated regarding the sequence, such as the unbroken winding and so forth, the wise one should recite all of that in the same manner within the jaṭā. 42.
In the *trikrama*, having uttered the matted locks (*jaṭā*) of even the third foot according to the rule (43),
one should then recite the second and subsequent feet there as before; wherever two feet are identical either in vowel or in consonant (44).

One should not recite the *jaṭā* [interlaced] form; rather, one should always recite it according to the sequence alone, including those instances of elision and non-elision, as well as the changes of *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*.
One should recite those features prescribed for the *jaṭā* according to the rule.
Those phonemes which are traditionally taught here according to the scriptures, characterized solely by the sequence of their letters,
one should pronounce all of them with the word "kāra" at the end when speaking of the sequence of letters. 46.
In this context, among the consonants (*hal*), the word *kāra* may be preceded by the letter *a*;
however, the word *kāra* is not desired after the nasalized *anusvāra*, the *nāsikya*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *visarga*, or the *upadhmānīya* sounds. (47–48)

In the case of the three [consonants] following a vowel, there may be a short vowel as the subsequent letter; however, in the recitation of the phonemes, no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) occurs between a vowel and a *kāra* suffix that follows it. He should utter those [consonants], along with the long vowels and the *visarga*, at the conclusion of the statement.
Since the sequence of phonemes was explained previously, one should first recite the *saṃhitā*.
For he who should utter the dry sequence of phonemes devoid of the *saṃhitā* would be as fruitless as painting a picture on a wall that lacks a surface.

That by which a sentence is determined— whether by a phoneme or by an accent— that very same [phoneme] one should pronounce in the recitations of individual letters (*varṇapāṭha*), and not as a *saṃhitā* [conjunction].
By this rule, the learned man should utter the sequences of phonemes in their proper order.
The section on doubling (dvitva): A consonant that follows a vowel (ac) preceded by another vowel shall undergo doubling;
likewise, a stop (sparśa) preceded by *l* or *v*, and that which follows the letter *r*. 53.

When the letters *ṅ* and *n* stand at the end of a word preceded by a short vowel, they undergo doubling even before a following vowel. (54) In this Vedic text (*Yajurveda*), that *anusvāra* which occurs here should be joined with half a letter *ga*; if there is a *śa* below it, it is accompanied by a similar [letter] above, and if there is a *śa* above it, it becomes *go*. (55)

A nasal *anusvāra* preceding a conjunct (*yoga*) and a short vowel (*hrasva*) followed by a consonant undergo reduplication; that [reduplicated element] shall have the duration of one *mātrā*. (56) Section on Augments (*āgama*).
When a consonant becomes doubled by means of a specific cause,
there shall indeed be a preceding insertion (pūrvāgama) in sequence for the second and fourth [consonants] therein;
provided that this doubling occurs within a single word between two vowels.
Those two would be known as "following the target" (lakṣyānusāra) and "by name" (saṃjñā), distinct from the [other] characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
58. On this path, those preceded by "ati," "adhi," and "su" are the most excellent among beings;
likewise, those preceded by prefixes (upasarga) arrived with the arms of friends. 59.

When a first *uṣman* (sibilant) follows, there is a substitution of the second [consonant] in the case of identical syllables; when the syllables are different, both letters [are substituted]. In the Taittirīya, a nasal preceded by *ś* becomes *ñ*, but not in the Kāṭhaka.
Thus ends the third chapter, the section on *abhinidhāna*.
When a voiceless sibilant (*ūṣman*) followed by a stop (*sparśa*) is situated after [another sound], [the preceding vowel is nasalized]. 61.
The first [consonant] shall undergo abhinidhāna, as shall its place of articulation (sthāna) when the suffixes śas or au follow; however, where these are the subsequent elements,
the mention of abhinidhāna does not apply there— the wise scholar should instead utter the first [consonant] twice.
The section on *kevalāgama*:
the letter *da* is low (*nīca*), preceded by [a vowel] and likewise high (*ucca*) when followed by a vowel; this is *kevalāgama*.
Similarly, in the following cases, the letters *ka* and *ga* are respectively the two *āgamas* occurring after a nasal (*ṅataḥ*) that is not final.
It would be [the *yama*] where, following an unsurpassed *sparśa*, there is a subsequent *uttama*;
in that case, the *yamas* would occur in sequence, provided there is no *antaḥstha* following it. (64) Section on *Yama*.

If touch were a modification of heat, then the [scriptural] injunction regarding *yama* would not apply there. Wherever the attainment of *yama* occurs, if heat were present there, then this would be a section concerning the prohibition of *yama*. (65)

In that case, there is no attainment of *yama*, nor does the *ūṣman* attain doubling. (66) That which is the first [consonant] at the end of a word, or before a sibilant (*ṣaṣ*) followed by another [consonant], attains doubling; likewise, if it is not final, it does so when followed by a sibilant (*ś*). (67)
Regarding the section on *nāda*:
whatever *nāda* occurs here following a short vowel, the wise man should utter it only once according to the sequence of phonemes in this chapter. 68.
The Section on the Prohibition of the Arrival of Duplication:
When the arrival of duplication characterized by a preceding element has occurred for a consonant (*hal*), that which was the preceding element is said to be withdrawn. (69)
The first *ūṣman* (sibilant) may optionally become double when followed by a vowel; likewise, *va*, *visarga*, and *ra* [may become double] before a stop (*sparśa*).
The letter *la* [becomes double] before an *ūṣman* or a stop, as do the vowels *ī*, *e*, *ai*, and *o*.

That [anusvāra] is the final of its own class when followed by a sibilant (ūṣman), and likewise the final of a consonant (hal) when followed by a sibilant; furthermore, if it follows *m*, *s*, *y*, *v*, or *l* and is followed by one of those [nasals], it becomes their respective nasalized counterpart (*anunāsika*).
When following a long vowel, it is optionally the final [of the word]; it does not double, nor does it occur before *n*, nor before a spirant (*vyavṛṇvra*).

Furthermore, neither the short nor the long [vowels] attain a doubling when followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) after *r* or *l*, because in that case, the *svarabhakti* is the object [of the doubling rule]. 73.

The vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ* may optionally be half-measures (*svarārdha*); therefore, they constitute the *svarabhakti*. That [svarabhakti], consisting of a vowel or a consonant, is joined with exactly four quarters (*pāda*). Among those quarters, the first and last quarters should consist of vowels.
The two feet that stand in the middle, however, should be known as consisting of consonants (vyañjana).
One should not join the second foot with the first foot;
rather, one should join the third foot with the fourth foot. 75–76.
In this manner, one should there divide the two feet sequentially, each separately.

The first portion shall consist of consonants (halanta), while its vowel-portion (svarabhakti) is closed (saṃvṛta). The subsequent portion shall be the vowel-portion (bhakti), which is open (vivṛta) and arises from the vowel.

The first half [of a svarabhakti] occurs before the letter *ha*, while the latter half likewise occurs before *cha*, *ṣa*, and *sa*. Furthermore, the *atva* (short *a*-quality), *itva* (short *i*-quality), and *utva* (short *u*-quality) that follow a *bhakti* vowel are designated as *svarabhakti*.
Without pronouncing this triad, one should utter the *svarabhakti*. If there is a conjunction of *ra* and *ha*, it is known as the *barhiḥ-kareṇu* designation;
in a conjunction of *la* and *ha*, it is to be known as the *sāmalhākarvaṇī*; and in a conjunction of *la* and *ka*, it is the *lahakāra*.
A *haṃsapadā* is to be known when there is a *ra* or a *ṣa* in the *yoga*; likewise, a *hariṇī* is [known] by an *ṛ* followed by an *u*.
A *darśa* is cited as having a *repha* (the letter *r*) and a *parśu* (the letter *p*). Where there is a *repha* followed by a *pa*, it is also called a *hastinī*. (81)
In cases such as *tasya dhūrṣadam*, that [svarabhakti] is declared to be independent;
when there is a conjunction of *l* and *ś*, it is called *hāritā*, as exemplified by *śatavālśam*.
In this manner, these seven svarabhaktis are easily understood in their proper sequence.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the definition of *vivṛtti*.
The opening (*vivṛtti*) of both vowels is called their *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction).

In this context, that very manifestation is also called "articulation" (vyakti). Furthermore, [the following types of recitation] have been described: the calf-following (vatsānusṛti), the calf-pursuing (vatsānusāriṇī), the Vaiśeṣikā, the Pākavatī, the Madhyamā, and the Pipīlikā. 84–85.
Likewise, the "long by homogeneous vowel" (*savarṇadīrghī*) and the "long by both" (*ubhayadīrghī*) are thus recorded;

in this way, there would be eight designations for the *vivṛtti* vowels according to their distinctions. Furthermore, there is the manifestation preceded by a short vowel, as well as that which has a long vowel following it.
That is called *vatsānusṛti*; it is equal in duration [to the preceding vowel] in terms of time.
That which occurs before a short vowel is a *vivṛtti*, and that which follows a protracted (*pluta*) or long (*dīrgha*) vowel is this *vatsānusāriṇī*, joined with a single *mātrā*. 87–88.

That [vowel] whose long [form] occurs at the beginning and end of its manifestation, provided that the two [long vowels] are of dissimilar phonetic quality (asavarṇa), and if there is a visarga in the middle—or if there is an absence thereof—is called Vaiśeṣikā; and in that case, it indeed possesses the measure of a half-mātrā. 89.
If there should be a short [syllable] both before and after, then it is known as *pādonamātrikā*, and that is called *pākavatī*.
That [verse] in which there are long syllables of the same color (vowel) at both the high and low [positions] is [also so defined]. 90–91.

In that case, the *visarga* is a *svāra*, and the *sandhi* consists of a middle *mātrā*. If the *visarga* does not occur there according to the definition, that manifestation (*vyakti*) is to be known as *pipīlikā*, measuring one quarter of a *mātrā*.
If there is a *savarṇadīrgha* at the beginning or at the end, it is distinct from the *visarga*;
if it is a *svarita* in the *sandhi*, it possesses one *mātrā*. That [vowel] belongs to the *savarṇadīrgha* when the full definition is satisfied. (93–94)
If there is no *visarga* therein, it is a long vowel of equal measure (*samātra*) for both;
now, examples of the *vivṛtti* [sandhi] are cited in sequence, with specific instances such as "vatsānusṛti" and so forth. 95.
There may be the designation *vatsānusṛti*; they have declared that this [hymn] is directed toward him. May this *vatsānusāriṇī* belong to Agni.
There may be the *vaiśeṣikā*; those very ones [are for] Kakṣīvat Auśija.

That [verse] is to be known as *pākavatī*, and that *prauga* is among the people (97). The nasalized sound in the middle of the syllable is said to have entered into the middle [vowel] of the *madhyamā*; "ādanya" is also [a term for it].
But for you, this [term] *pipīlikā* is cited as being forest-dwelling (āraṇya).

Because we see examples such as *sa-varṇa-dīrghī*, *saṃyuktā*, and *āsannā*, this [term *pipīlikā*] would have to be one where both [vowels] are long; or else, it might be that water (*āpaḥ*) is likewise [treated]. 98–99.
That nasal sound which occurs in the middle of a manifest vowel is of the measure of an atom (sāṇumātrika).
Indeed, the atomic nature of the manifest vowel has already been explained previously. (100) [This concludes] the section on the *raṅgapluta* vowels.
Yaśomā, upahūtā, suślokā, sumaṅgalā—these are to be known as raṅgapluta; likewise is that which begins with "yadghrām.
In the raṅgapluta, there should be two morae at the beginning, resembling the roar of a tiger.
The first [vibration] arises from the heart, is without sound, and is accompanied by a low resonance (mandra-dhvani). Then, in the middle portion, there is the third, which originates from the head;
it is equal to the sound of a bronze bell, vibratory, and consists of a single measure (mātrā). 102–103.
Now, at the final portion, that which issues from the two nostrils as a quarter-measure (*mātrā*) is the *kākalika*;
it is like the cowherd girl of Saurāṣṭra with her sweet voice. 104.
One should pronounce "takrām" loudly, and likewise one should pronounce "raṅgam. (105) This is the section on the long *raṅga*.
"The gods, indeed, [are] immortal, [they are] our protectors," thus [it is said] in the Kāṭhaka.
Those [vowels] are said to be "long by nature" (raṅgadīrghāḥ), consisting of three and a quarter mātrās. Among them, the one born from the heart (the short *a*) consists of one mātrā;
that which is born from the head (*u*) consists of half a mātrā; and the remainder is produced from the mouth and nose (*m*).
Thus ends the fifth chapter concerning the scope of the circumflex, acute, and tremulous accents:
these [vowels] are circumflex by virtue of being inherent (nitya), abhinihita, kṣaipra, or praśliṣṭa.
In that junction where high-pitched svarita syllables arise, they tremble.
One should make the following syllable low at the end of the preceding vowel; that indeed is the "tremor" (kaṃpa).
Even in this case of tremor, one should pronounce a short vowel as if it were long.
And that *kaṃpa* (tremor) here should be understood as being of two kinds: *svāra-kaṃpa* and *ucca-kaṃpa*.

The *svāra-kaṃpa* occurs in the *saṃhitā* [text] due to the high pitch (*uccastva*), while in the *Āraṇyaka* it would be [the other]. Furthermore, those two *kaṃpas* there are traditionally known as short (*hrasva*) and long (*dīrgha*).
At the beginning of that kampita, the svarita is said to have one and a half mātrās;
at its end, however, it is suppressed and proclaimed to have the measure of one quarter (pāda).
And likewise, at the beginning of the udātta, it has more than three-quarter mātrās.
At its end there should be an *anudātta* (unaccented) tone, and it should likewise be of the measure of an atom (*aṇumātra*).
Upon their union, it becomes two measures (*dvimātra*); thus is it well-ascertained for both the modified (*vaikṛta*) and the natural (*prākṛta*) [sounds]. 113.
Vaikṛta, Prākṛta, and so forth.
When a visarga is seen before the letters śa, ṣa, or sa, there is a modification;

for in such a case, the preceding [visarga] is indeed *prākṛta* (original) and the subsequent [letters] are *vaikṛta* (modified), occurring in close conjunction (*śliṣṭa*). Furthermore, when the letters ṇa, na, ma, ya, ra, or la are seen following the letter ha, [the same applies].
The qualities of being nasal (*nāsikyatva*) and being chest-born (*urasyatva*), and so forth— namely, nasality and chest-bornness— are stated twice there for the letter *ha*.
Wherever a visarga occurs between two open vowels (*vivṛtti*), it possesses half a mora (*ardhamātrika*).
A pause (virāma) shall consist of one mātrā; its designation is according to the rule:
if there is a visarga preceded by a non-aspirated consonant and followed by a non-aspirated consonant or a labial (ka-pavarga), it is termed jihvāmūlīya, and so forth.
In due order, that [visarga] is called *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*. When the letter *ka* follows a *ṣavara*,
there occurs the *sthitisaṃdhi* (the sandhi of retention).
The visarga situated before [the following vowel] is known as the *sthitisandhi*. 118.
The name of a phoneme (*varṇa*) devoid of a vowel is said to be its designator;
during the study of the sequence of phonemes, one should not utter another name for it. 119.

An anusvāra known as *kevala* that stands in the middle [of a word] does not undergo doubling even when followed by a rule-applying consonant (*vidhi*) or a conjunct (*yoga*); this is the prohibition of doubling for the initial *oṃkāra* and others in the context of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). 120. This is the prohibition of doubling for the initial *oṃkāra* and so forth.
At the beginning, in the initial *oṃkāra*, the letter *a* consists of one foot-measure (*mātrā*);
it becomes two measures for three feet; the letter *u* is likewise one measure;
and at the end of a chapter or the end of a section (*anuvāka*), the letter *m* consists of half a measure.
In the recitations following the sequence of phonemes,
there shall be no euphonic combination (sandhi) between a vowel and a following *kāra* suffix, nor even in the middle of the *praṇava*, nor in the case of protracted vowels (*pluta*).
This is the characteristic of the sequence of vowels and phonemes.
While that sequence of pure phonemes is being recited in its proper order,
there are three accents— namely the udātta, the anudātta, and the pracaya— as well as seven svarita accents, each produced with its specific effort and bearing its own name. (123–124)

If one were to apply these ten [vowels] here and there according to the sounds and utter them by name, this would be the sequence of vowels and phonemes; it is the designation for the acute (udātta) and the other accents. 125.
This is the definition of the acute and so forth.

When describing phonemes (varṇas), one should not mention accents such as the udātta; for in that context, the udātta and others are themselves the designators of those [phonemes]. Now, the articulatory efforts (prayatnas) are being defined in their proper sequence according to the rule. 126.
A vowel pronounced with high pitch is called udātta (acute), while one struck down by low pitch is anudātta (grave). A combination of these two is svarita (circumflex), which is also termed svāra;
this occurs when there are following anudātta vowels within the same word following a svarita.
In the *saṃhitā*, however, the *pracaya* accent is held to be audible;
furthermore, the terms *dhṛta* and *pracaya* are synonyms for one another.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
The characteristics of the seven accents:
the *svarita* accents are to be known as sevenfold, and their efforts (*prayatna*) are fourfold.
The first *svarita* is the *kṣaipra*; the second is designated as *nitya*. (130)

The third is *prātihata*, and the fourth is twofold by name: therein one is known as *abhinihata* and the other as *abhihata*. The fifth is *praśliṣṭa*, and the sixth is *vṛtta*, which consists of the *pādavṛttaka*.
That which is a svarita and would be the seventh [syllable] is known as *tairovyañjana*. When there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel *i*, the combination is pronounced with a high pitch;
that is the *kṣaipra* accent, as in the examples *tryambakam* and *drvannaḥ*. (132–133)

Whether it occurs in a word-final position, in an *apūrva* (unprecedented) context, or following a low-pitched syllable, where a syllable is always intoned with a high pitch, it is cited as *nyañc* (downward), as in the case of *kuhvā*. Furthermore, that which is intoned with a high pitch even when situated in various words by means of a *śliṣṭa* (conjoined) accent is likewise [treated].
That [word] would indeed be subject to contradiction;
for here among us, that which is pronounced high first and then low on various syllables—whether in the absence or presence of a distinct phonetic manifestation—is held to be contradicted. 135–136.
If there is the elision of the letter *a* in that case where the words have become separate, then it should be known as the *svāra-abhinihata*; he said "te" even though they had not spoken.
If that [elided *a*] was preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*) and is pronounced with the *ūbhāva* [svarita] tone, then [it is so].
That which is called *praśliṣṭa* is well-chanted by a skilled *udgātṛ*, just as a well-guided horse [follows its path].
When there is a manifestation (*vyakti*) within an uninterrupted word (*akhaṇḍapada*), it should be half a *mātrā* in duration;
that which follows it is the *svāra* (svarita) known as *pādavṛtta*. 138–139.

That manifestation which occurs in the middle of a foot, and which possesses a *svarita* accent, is alone considered a *pādavṛtta*; no other is desired as such. (140) That which is called "transverse" (*tiras*) is known as a consonant (*hal-vyañjana*).
That *svarita* which is separated from its own vowel by a consonant is designated as *tairovyañjana*.
When it occurs within a word (*pade*), being preceded by an acute (*udātta*) vowel and separated from it by a consonant,
that very same *svarita* is called *tairovyañjana*.

That *svarita* which is pronounced with a high pitch (*ucca*) immediately following [the preceding vowel] within the same word is to be known as *tairovyañjana*; thus, "āpo vācamupāyavaḥ" [is an example].
This is the distinction in effort among the various *svarita* tones.
In the case of a *kṣaipra* sandhi, the effort should be constant; in the case of a *svāra*, it should be even firmer.

When an *abhinihata* occurs preceded by a low tone (*nīca*), the effort is traditionally held to be very firm; when preceded by a high tone (*ucca*) or not preceded at all, a firm effort is likewise required. (143)

That [intonation] which occurs in the *praśliṣṭa* and *pratihata* [svaritas] is indeed considered the softest (mṛdutara). That which occurs in the *tairovyañjana* and in the *pādavṛtta* is considered slightly less so (alpatara).
Thus, [the distinctions arise] from the differences in the types of svarita and the efforts (*prayatna*) involved.
The defining characteristics of these have been stated according to the scriptures based on the intention [of the author].
Having understood all of this—the sequence of vowels and consonants—one should speak; such is the definition of the sequence of phonemes according to the duration of the measures (mātrās). 146.

Now, therefore, in this chapter on the Saṃhitā, according to their characteristics and in their proper sequence, whatever [rules] there are for the phonemes and whatever their durations are well-determined,
all of those [are applied] to each respective vowel and consonant according to the rule. 147.
If they are employed before the accents such as the udātta,
and if the order of recitation were thus, then a syllable is said to consist of one mātrā;
[this concludes] the seventh chapter.
The characteristics of the duration of time for the *mātrās* are now stated individually according to their causes:
the Brāhmaṇī, the Cāṣa bird, the crow, and the peacock, respectively. (149)

They say that [the syllables] consisting of one, two, or three morae (mātrās) are easy to pronounce according to their duration. That which is beyond the range of the senses is called an *aṇu* by the wise; four such *aṇus* are traditionally known as a *mātrā* in terms of measurement.

A short vowel should consist of one measure (mātrā), while a long vowel should consist of two measures. A protracted (pluta) vowel is to be known as consisting of three measures; half of a short vowel, however, consists of half a measure.
In that context, a protracted vowel used on the stage is said to consist of four measures.

But that bell-sound which follows at the end of the tiger's roar (vyāghraruta), characterized by the discernment of the duration of the morae (mātrākāla) and the utterance [of the consonant], whether it be joined with or unjoined from another vowel— if that consonant possesses a vowel [as its inherent sound], [it is considered a long syllable]. 153.
One should speak of the duration of the vowel there, but not separately for the consonant (154).

Even though it possesses the measure of half an atom, one should still not speak of its duration as being separate from the vowel, nor likewise [as separate] from the *ha*-class consonants, within the sequence of phonemes (155).
Wherever there is a pause (hal) in these [syllables], that is considered their duration;
however, in the case of the *anuttama* [svaras], a pause of half a mora (*ardhamātra*) is prescribed.
In the case of the *uttama* [svaras] occurring at a pause, an increase in duration is observed.

That which follows a short vowel preceded by a nasal is said to have two morae (mātrās). According to the Śruti, that which follows a long or protracted (pluta) vowel has one mora and possesses resonance (nāda).
This is a distinction at the pause (avasāna) that does not exist for other [sounds]. 157–158.
In the *saṃhitā*, however, that [vowel] alone is present; at the time of the *pada* text, it becomes longer;
and when following a short vowel and standing at the end of a word (*avasāna*), it is nasalized in the *padapāṭha*.
It consists of two morae (*dvimātra*), while the other is one mora (*mātrika*); likewise, in the *saṃhitā*, there is the *khila* (the protracted vowel).
Having thus understood those respective times, one should utter the phonemes according to their measure (mātraka). This is the characteristic of the sequence of the phonemes of the limbs (aṅgavarṇa):
in the phonemes of the limbs, at the beginning of the consonants (hal), there is the limb, the designation (saṃjñā), and the name.
One should state the name of the vowel, its designation, its measure, and its accent in sequence (161).
In this system of limb-colors for the phonemes, the characteristic of the limbs is clearly expressed; it is stated according to the rule of either priority or posteriority (162).
Because it shines by itself, it is called *svara* (vowel);
because it is manifested by that which stands above it (*adhi*), it is called *vyañjana* (consonant). This is the definition of the limbs (*aṅga*). 163.
It is not possible for a consonant to stand alone without a vowel;
the consonant is always dependent, whereas the vowel is independent. Indeed, all consonants are limbs of the vowel.

A consonant generally belongs to the following vowel as its constituent part; however, that which stands at the end of a word belongs to the preceding vowel. 165. Thus ends the section on the characteristics of the preceding and following limbs [of the syllable].
The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, and the *bhakti* are [the final elements] of a conjunct consonant (*yukta*).
166. When followed by a vowel (*ṛpara*), the *ṅa*, *na*, or *repha* (r) that is not joined with another [consonant] at the beginning of a word (*yogādyasaṃyuta*) becomes [an anusvāra].
167. A *sparśa* (stop) does not become the preceding member if it is a modification of a *ūṣman* (sibilant).
That devotion which is supreme through its accumulation indeed becomes a subordinate member (*parāṅga*).

For when the vowel *ṛ* is held, the following *r* should likewise be a subordinate member; and that which is a semi-vowel (*antasthā*) following [the vowel] is a non-homogeneous subordinate member. 168–169.
When the *parāṅga* (the subsequent member) is followed by a *sparśa* (stop consonant), *ūṣman* (sibilant), or another *parāṅga*, the *yamāḥ* (nasal counterparts) are applied.
Having understood the characteristic of the sequence of the limbs (*aṅga*) and phonemes (*varṇa*) through their very order of precedence and succession, one should employ the limb accordingly. 170
Having uttered either the word "pūrva" or the word "para," one should then sequentially utter the word "aṅga" followed by the word "bhūta"; then,
one should state the designation "hal-saṃjñaka" followed by the vowel of the name.
Having stated that [the consonants] are designated as *acāmac* (vowels), he should then recite those vowels—namely the *udātta* and so forth—and thereafter the names in their proper sequence;
provided that where there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the preceding member consists of a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*). 172–173.
In that case, one should pronounce it only once; thereafter, one should recite the preceding auxiliary (*pūrvāṅga*) and so forth.
Where the conjunction consists of both auxiliaries and is composed of a single consonant, one should apply the individual auxiliaries there according to the sequence of priority and posteriority.
Whatever was stated regarding the pure phonemes— such as the occurrence of doubling and so forth—
all of that should be declared in due order for each respective limb-phoneme, just as the vowels were established by their characteristics in the section on vowel-phonemes. (175–176)

The wise man should state all those *mātrās* and *mātrikās* which have been determined for each phoneme (*varṇa*) exactly as they are in that context, when speaking of the phonemes of the limbs (*aṅga*). 177.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
The etymological explanation of the sequence of the essences of the phonemes (varṇasāra):
For all phonemes, the "essence" (sāra), the "path" (adhvan), and so forth are traditionally taught;
those which are the "resonance" (dhvani), the "place of articulation" (sthāna), and so forth, are proclaimed as their "properties" (dharma). (178)
The word *bhūta* here refers to that which has been brought about by them through the word *bhūta*;

it is thus described. Furthermore, the analysis of the compound *varṇakrama*—as "the sequence of phonemes" (*varṇānāṃ kramaḥ*) and "that which is this sequence of phonemes" (*sa ca asau varṇakramaḥ*)—has been made clear.
Therefore, this sequence of phonemes (varṇakrama), which is considered the essence of phonemes, is traditionally taught as the sequence of phonemic properties (varṇadharmakrama);
it applies to a single vowel, even when it is joined with an initial consonant and accompanied by other consonants.
Twenty-six properties have been declared; thus it has been asked: "What is it?
Here, it is the word itself that is called *dhvani* by its characteristics. Thus, *dhvani* is the first property, while the second position is said to be [the locus]. 181–182.
One should know the third to be the instrument (*karaṇa*); the fourth would be effort (*prayatna*);
the fifth is to be known as the deity (*devatā*); the sixth is here called the genus (*jāti*).
The seventh is declared to be the limb (*aṅga*), while the eighth would be the designation of the phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñā*). (183)

These phonetic elements (dharmas) are prescribed here in their proper sequence. Even while this group of eight dharmas is being explained in order, the duration of the mora (mātrākāla) must be stated between the deity (deva) and the effort (prayatna). 184–185.
Ten characteristics have been proclaimed for the vowels, beginning with the *nihata* (suppressed) and so forth.

Among these, first the deity is to be known, then the genus (*jāti*), then the quality (*guṇa*), then the line (*rekhā*), then the appearance (*darśana*), and finally the threefold state of the limbs (*aṅgāvasthā*). 186.

Then there would be the cause of the *ṣaḍja* and other notes, and then their place of origin; then their designations—these ten factors one should state in sequence as they are taught regarding the four categories of pure notes (*svara*), measures (*mātra*), limbs (*aṅga*), and syllables (*varṇa*). 187–188.
One should apply all those various dharmas and recite them in this sequence; whatever dharma occurs as the fifth in the *Acām-varṇasāraka*—
thus ends the ninth chapter.

The object of the *anusvāra*-portion and the *kampita* [intonation] would be the vowels that constitute parts of the *svarabhakti*, for it is the seventh [note]; [this applies] even to the *jhaḷ* consonants that are parts of the portions of the *anusvāra*. 190.
One should always describe the phonemes *dh*, *ny*, *th*, *v*, *dhy*, and so forth according to their true nature in the *Varṇasāra*.
In this case of the phoneme *anusvāra*, one should first state the *mātrikā* from the *aṅga*;
furthermore, regarding the portion that is a part of the *anusvāra*, one should sequentially state the *dharma*s of the *vyaṅga*s.

When there is trembling caused by that [recitation], one should then recite the dharmas of one's own *svāra* at the beginning. However, for one who has experienced trembling, one should not recite the dharmas of one's own *svāra* for the initial portion of that [trembling], which lasts for more than three *mātrās*. 192–193.
One should state the rules for the final portion of the base [color] according to the prescribed method;
just as it was applied there for the pure color, so too should one apply it here. (194) This concerns the subject of the flooding of colors (*raṅga-pluta*).

When there is a prolated vowel (*pluta*) following a short vowel (*avarṇa*), one should state the phonetic properties (*dharma*) of the prolated vowels in their proper sequence within the *Varṇasāra*. At the end of that, one should state those designated as "vowels" (*varṇasaṃjñaka*). Furthermore, that which is called *abhinidhāna* occurs everywhere, and its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are likewise.
One may speak even of the perception of color (varṇa-saṃjñā), but one should never recite other dharmas.
One should not speak of sounds and so forth; however, the *Sthānāṅga*, which is the section concerning the production of sound, is not prohibited. 196.
Now, for the sake of establishing the correct pronunciation of all classes of people, and especially for those belonging to the Yajurveda, the origin of sound is described here:
generally, sound may be considered in two ways—as eternal or as an effect. (197–198)
Sound is eternal, manifest, and all-pervasive; it is that which receives the designation of Brahman.
Therefore, the manifest sound of effects arises from the effect;
from the *śruti* comes the *nāda*, from that the *nālī*, and from the *nālī* arise the various high and low tones. (199)
In the section defining *dhvani*, the abiding of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) within the body is described:
"These [vital airs] arise in succession merely from the utterance of sound;
their mutual distinctness is like that of light and its radiance. (200)
The causes for the articulation of phonemes, headed by sound (nāda), arise;

at the emergence of the navel, the subtle channel (sūkṣmadhamanī) forms a knot-like connection, which serves as the support for all the elements (dhātu) as well as for the sense faculties (indriya). 201–202.
That [channel], though thick enough to be immersed by the palm, is raised half a finger-breadth high;
it is constantly motionless and blazing like a gastric flame,
and situated within it is a vein as subtle as a supreme atom, covered with a veil.

Thus ends the tenth chapter. [It describes] the locations, stations, and so forth of the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa; and how the channels, filled by the wind, move swiftly and incessantly. (204)
The prāṇa, udāna, apāna, and samāna are established in the heart, throat, anus, and navel respectively; the vyāna is situated throughout all the limbs.
These five, remaining there, each consist of three parts. 205.
In this body, two by two, they perform their respective functions.
Residing in the wheel of equal apertures, the wind protects the sacrificial grass; supported by the creeper-like channels, it stays at the base of the sling above the triple-junction.
Having first separated the excretions and urine, the *vyāna* wind, circulating everywhere by resorting to all the channels, subsequently casts them downward;
it always pervades everything, yet it does not perform such acts as the lifting up of the mind. 208.
The *udāna* wind, situated in the throat-passage,

having leaped up from the root of the tongue and seized the essence and other nutrients brought by the *vyāna*, casts them downward into the interior located behind the pericarp of the heart-lotus, which is densely packed with the tubes of the channels. (209–210)

Abiding in its own place, the powerful vital breath (prāṇa), through contractions and expansions in due order, spontaneously grants the supreme path to both enjoyment and liberation. The distinction among these lies in their gross and subtle forms and activities.
These activities of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others are gross; now their subtle form is described:
by means of its own portion residing in the heart, the prāṇa draws inward from outside the portion of udāna residing in the throat, and that portion of it [gradually] proceeds in sequence.
The body is sustained by both parts in the form of breath.
When one desires to speak, the mind, rising upward, draws up the air from the throat;
that [air], having struck [the fire] and fallen into the digestive fire, is then raised by the heat produced therein.
Then, by means of the flame that pierces, one quickly breaks through the veil of the *samāna* fire; once the enclosure is pierced, the *prāṇa*, together with the mind and the wind,
directs its own portion into the region between the throat and the eyebrows.
The *prakṛti* (source) consists of the auditory organ and so forth; it is the effect, and from the eternal [word-principle] sound is produced here.

Its location is the middle between the throat and the chest; the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the balanced breath; the application is the mind, and its effort is the exertion—such is the production of sound. (216–217)
When these sounds, which obstruct the breath, are thus being uttered,
having drawn [the breath] evenly and uninterruptedly and joined it with the *udāna*,
as that mind rises up, the body is unable to endure its lack of movement. (218)

Furthermore, within the center, that vital breath (prāṇa) falls by its own portion alone; therefore, it is severed there by the friction of the vital breaths. Having its flow interrupted, it quickly becomes situated within its own place.
Immediately, the *prāṇa* and *udāna* [vital breaths] obstruct the reality-element (*tattva*) as before;
then, through their activity, a great gasping arises. Furthermore, by the application of the mind, sound is likewise produced.
That which has reached the space of the throat is to be understood as sound alone; it is traditionally known as *dhvani*.
The varieties of *dhvani*—namely the phonemes born from that, *nāda*, *śvāsa*, and the letter *ha*—thus constitute the threefold *dhvani*.

When the throat is constricted, there is sound (nāda) and breath; when it is open, there is the letter *ha*. These are the primary elements of the phonemes (*varṇaprakṛti*). The resonant sounds of the vowels (*svaraghoṣa*) are born from *nāda*, while those beginning with the fourth [sibilant] are born from the letter *ha*.
There, breath arising from the unvoiced [consonants] is twofold: short and long;
and the vowels, both initial and otherwise, arise as short and long.
This is the definition of the distinction between the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*) of the phonemes.
The place (*sthāna*) is the point of contact where another limb is extended;
that limb which is brought near the place is the instrument (*karaṇa*). When one limb is touched by another limb, that [latter] is held to be the place of the consonants (*hal*).
That part of the body by which a place is touched is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the *hal* (consonants).
Where vowels are always preceded by consonants in a *saṃhitā*, when their place of articulation is to be stated, one should first say "throat" (*kaṇṭha*). 227–228.
When pronouncing the letter *a*, the lips and jaws should be brought very close together;
however, for the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, these should not be too widely opened. When uttering the *i*-vowels, the middle of the tongue should be pressed against the palate.

The two lips should be long in the vowel *u* and likewise joined closely together (230). The contraction of the lips should not occur with an interval of half a *mātrā*; rather, there should be an interval of one *mātrā*, provided that it is possible in all cases (231).
In the vowel *ṛ*, the lips should be slightly closed, and the jaws should not be excessively drawn together;
the tip of the tongue should be short.
In the consonant *e*, the edges of the tongue should be slightly joined with the lips. (232)
The organ is the palate, and the place of articulation is the upper part of the jaw joined closely together (233).
When this [palate] is accompanied by a consonant, the pair of lips should be slightly joined.
For the middle of the tongue, the place of articulation is the palate joined very closely with the jaw (234).
When the jaws are not excessively separated and the lips are very closely drawn together, and they become elongated, then upon the utterance of the vowel *u*,
one should pronounce it as *aṇu* at the beginning; however, when it occurs at the end, it is *tryaṇuka* for the vowels *i* and *u*.
In the vowels *ai* and *au*, the initial *a* consists of half a mora (236).
The remaining portions of the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels each consist of one and a half morae, corresponding respectively to the *at* and *ut* components within the parts of *ai* and *au*. (237)
The effort (*prayatna*) involved in the production of *a* and *i* is exactly the same as that for *e* and *o*, and not otherwise;
even the slightest trace of *a* or *i* is not heard here separately. This is not because those [efforts] do not exist in it, but rather because it possesses the qualities of *aitva* and *autva*.
Those expert in the sequence of phonemes say that at the beginning, the organ of articulation for the letter *a* and its like is the lips, and it is called "closed" (*saṃvṛta*).
When pronouncing the *ka*-group, the wise person should touch the root of the jaw.
The *u* sound is uttered with the root of the tongue, and the *ū* sound with the middle of the tongue against the palate;

the *ṭa*-group is produced by the tip of the tongue while touching the head [the roof of the mouth]. The *ta*-group is produced by the tip of the tongue against the roots of the teeth, and likewise below [for the *da*-group].
Then, for the pronunciation of the *pavarga* [consonants], one should touch the upper lip with the tip of the tongue (242).
For the pronunciation of the palatals (*tālavya*), one should touch [the palate] with the sides of the middle of the tongue;
for the dentals (*dantamūla*), one should move the middle of the tip of the tongue over the roots of the teeth (243).
One should touch the region near and very close to the *ra* and *la* sounds with the outer part of the tip of the lower lip; one should not touch it above [the teeth].
If the vowel *u* stands between [the consonants], it is like the labial vowels; however, if it is different from that, it is done by means of the inner [part of the lip]. 244.

The points of articulation for the jihvāmūlīya, for the consonants other than *ha*, and likewise for the sibilants (*ūṣman*), should be the same as those of the [consonants] beginning with the *ka*-group, respectively;
however, among their causes, that which is in the middle should be wide open (*vivṛta*). 245–246.
The place of articulation and the organ for the visarga and the letter *ha* are the throat;
however, when followed by a voiceless unaspirated stop (*uttama*) or a semivowel (*antasthā*), both of these [the throat and the chest] are the organs.
When followed by the final letters of the classes (*vargāntya*) or the nasal (*nāsikāmātra*), they have the same places of articulation as those [following sounds]. (247)

"Of one who exists, the nasal [sound] belongs to the nose as a part of the mouth, while the non-nasal [sounds] belong to the nose itself. (248) Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Analysis of Places and Articulators."
The efforts regarding the articulation of phonemes (varṇa) are to be known as fivefold:
the closed (saṃvṛta), the open (vivṛta), the touched (spṛṣṭa), the slightly touched (īṣatspṛṣṭa), and that preceded by the [open] (atipūrvaka). 249
The effort for the *kāra* (the vowel *a*) alone is proclaimed to be "contracted" (*saṃvṛta*);
the effort for other vowels as well as for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is "open" (*vivṛta*).
Among the stops (*sparśa*), "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*) is declared, while for the semivowels (*antasthā*), there is "slight contact" (*īṣatspṛṣṭatva*). 250.
The second and fourth [consonants] are produced with the effort of *atispṛṣṭa* (excessive contact).
In the case of *atispṛṣṛṣṭa*, a slight deficiency is admitted for the fourth [consonants].
[Now follows] the determination of the deities and castes (*jāti*) of the vowels and consonants.
The deities of the Vedic letters are wind (vāyu), fire (agni), earth (kṣmā), moon (indu), and sun (bhānu).
The first two letters of the *yaśa* group belong to the deity Wind; the second two letters belong to the deity Fire, as do the letters *ra* and *ṣa*. (252)
The vowels *u*, the third [vowels] (*i*, *ī*, *e*), and *l* belong to the Earth-gods (Bhūmidevas);
the vowel *ṛ*, the fourth [vowels] (*u*, *ū*, *o*), and *v* are remembered as belonging to the Moon;
those beginning with *lṛ* and the final letters (*kṣa*) belong to the Sun; but for the others, there are no presiding deities. 253
The first letters of each varga and the vowels belong to the Brahmin caste;
the second, third, and fourth [letters of each varga], as well as the semivowels (*antastha*) and the last [letters of each varga], belong to the Kṣatriya caste;
and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), the visarga, and the anusvāra are determined to be Śūdras. 254.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter: Designations of Phonemes.
Vowels (ac) are the *svara*s; consonants (*hal*) consist of the *sparśa*s, *antastha*s, and *ūṣman*s. 255.
The first letters of the voiceless and voiced classes, the first and last [letters] of each class,

the short, long, and protracted vowels, the *bhakti* (fractional) consonants, the *paraṅga-pluta* (protracted at the end of a word), the *yamas*, as well as the *visarga*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and so forth. 256.
These, beginning with the *anusvāra*, are traditionally known as the designations for phonemes (*varṇa*).
The deities of the acute (*udātta*) and other accents are, in this context, the Sun, Fire, Moon, and Earth—these four—characterized respectively by their genus and qualities. 257.
The deities of the *dhṛta*, *anudātta*, *svāra*, and *ucca* accents are traditionally recorded as follows:
the four accents—namely *ucca*, *nīca*, *svāra*, and *dhṛta*—were, according to their respective order, the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra by birth in this world. (258–259)

That which possesses the *sattva* quality is known as *ucca-svarita*; that which possesses the *rajas* quality is remembered as *anudātta*; and those possessing the *tamas* quality are likewise held to be *dhṛta*. (260) This is the definition of the placement of hand gestures and vocal tones.
The wise person who performs the placement of the vowels (*svaranyāsa*), being seated and unwearied,
should place his right hand like a cow's ear upon his right knee; then,
he should sequentially fix his mind and sight upon the vowels and upon the hand.
One should place [the hand] on the tip of the big toe according to the instructions of the scripture.
At that time, if a venerable Guru or even a deity has arrived,
one should bow and then, while standing, place the hand level with the navel and perform the placement.
If permitted by them, when he has performed his practice,
he should remain seated and perform the placement of the vowels (*svaranyāsa*) according to the rule:
he should indicate the acute accent (*udātta*) on the middle joint of the index finger during the placement.

One should hold [the hand] low at the little finger and so forth, and in the middle of the middle finger; one should assign the *svaras* (musical notes) everywhere in this manner: the *svara* that occurs in its respective division shall attain its place in the *svara*. 265–266.
Where there is a *svāra* as if it were high (*ucca*), and that which is situated above,
one should place those two respectively on the ring finger and the middle finger. In the tremor of the *svāra*, there are the initial and final portions which constitute the *svāra-nīca*.
One should place those two [syllables] in sequence on the ring finger and the first finger (the thumb).

Then, one should likewise indicate those two [syllables] in sequence on the middle finger and the forefinger, corresponding respectively to the high-pitched tone with vibration (*udāttakampa*) and the raised and lowered positions (*uccanīcatau*). 268–269.
Regarding the result of the arrangement of vowels:
when there is a pause (*virāma*), whatever consonant occurs may, by virtue of its pronunciation, sometimes correctly acquire the sound of another vowel, as if it were independent. 270
Nevertheless, one should not specify a separate location for its placement;

rather, he who thus reflects upon the meanings of the vowels and consonants according to the perspective of the scriptures should recite this Veda precisely according to the sequence of vowel-placement (svaranyāsa). 271.
Purified by all the Vedas, he attains the Supreme Brahman. (272) [The characteristics of the state of *aṅga* and so forth are:
the lengthening of the limbs, firmness of the sound, and likewise the subtlety of the space in the throat.
In this regard, there are three conditions that produce sound loudly:
namely, the shortness of the body, the softness [of the vocal organs], and the great magnitude of the space of the throat; these produce sound softly. (273–274)
An exposition of the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja:
from the low [register] arise Ṣaḍja and Ṛṣabha; from the high [register] arise Gāndhāra and Madhyama; and Niṣāda, Pañcama, and Dhaivata are the three notes [of the middle register]. (275)
Among those, the sequence of causes for the origin of the *svarita* accent is as follows:
the *nitya*, *abhinihata*, and *kṣaipra* [svaritas] are the causes of the *niṣāda* note;
both the *hata* and *śliṣṭa* [svaritas] are caused by the *pañcama* note. (276)
The *dhaivata* note is born from the *tairovyañjana* and *vṛtta* accents (277).
Both *ṣaḍja* and *ṛṣabha* are born from the long, short, and *anudātta* accents;
likewise, *gāndhāra* and *madhyama* are born from the *udātta* and *pracaya* accents (278).
The female crane utters the *rauti* note, the *krauñca* bird the *gāndhāra* and *madhyama* notes in succession;
the peacock’s cry is like the *ṣaḍja*, the bull utters the *ṛṣabha* tone,
the pot-bellied elephant trumpets the *niṣāda*, and the cuckoo warbles the *pañcama*.
One should recognize the Dhaivata note as having a form similar to the neighing of a horse.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter:
"The Source of the Production of Accents such as Udātta."
The *anudātta* (unaccented) is to be known as being in the heart; the *udātta* (elevated) is declared to be in the head;
the *svarita* (circumflex) is at the root of the ear; and the *pracaya* (continuous) is remembered as being in all the limbs. [281] The fruit of Vedic study is this.
Those factors such as the *aṅgas* and others which have already been mentioned—let him apply all of them here and there in this *Varṇasāra*.
Thus, he who studies or even teaches this Veda characterized in this way [attains the fruit]. 282.
The fruit of that cannot be described even in thousands of kalpas.
The Veda is the greatness;
the Veda alone is the supreme dharma; the Veda alone is the supreme austerity.
The Veda alone is the supreme Brahman; the entire universe is composed of the Veda.
Therefore, in order to attain the highest good, this eternal dharma must be studied according to the prescribed rules from the mouth of a guru by all Brahmins. (284–285)

If one who is free from the fault of neglecting Vedic study should, in accordance with dharma, impart this Brahmic knowledge to a disciple, all the deities rejoice; no fear shall enter that brahmin. 286

That Brahmin who, having abandoned the Vedas, applies himself to other texts, should be known as a renouncer of Brahman; he is remembered in the Smṛti as a Śūdra in action. (287) The proficiency in all the scriptures of a Brahmin devoid of the Veda [is of no avail].

Just as a body devoid of clothing attains the state of being fully adorned [by its very nakedness], so too, O Brahmin, when one who possesses the form of a womb— that is, a Brahmin— engages in eating [forbidden food],
that Brahmin certainly incurs the fruit of drinking liquor. 288–289.

Then he obtains that supreme purification which belongs to the *nirākṛti*; therefore, one should not commit the sin of eating in the company of a *nirākṛti*. (290) *Nirākṛti* means one who is devoid of Vedic study.
Those men who revile the Vedas and the learned Brahmins shall fall into a terrible hell and be born as pigs on earth;
such is the fruit of studying the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga).
Those best of the twice-born who recite, according to the prescribed rite, that which is higher than the highest and shines forth in the form of the Veda,
shall experience the three aims of life here in this world and attain that supreme, eternal state.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter.
Thus ends the Ātreya-śikṣāmūla.
